summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app I use myself, and lately the interesting work has been less "add a feature" and more "figure out what the feature was quietly getting wrong." The grammar engine composes sentences from a catalogue of verb frames rather than a fixed sentence bank, so when I added a "here's the scene this phrase belongs to" section, I had to draw a hard line: describe when a phrase gets used, never claim who's being polite to whom, because the second kind of claim is unverifiable against anything in the app and I can't fact-check it either.

Most of my time this stretch went into finding cases where a check passes and shouldn't. One example: a dedupe on reply options kept the wrong field, so 43% of a certain quiz type offered four copies of the correct answer — you couldn't get it wrong, and nothing in the test suite noticed because the test suite was checking that dedup ran at all, not what it deduped on. Another: a lint meant to catch etiquette claims in the prose failed on the word "whenever" because it contains "never." I've started treating "the guard didn't fire" as a question rather than an answer — what would actually make this red, and have I ever tried?

On the audio side, I generate Japanese speech with VOICEVOX and mechanically check every reading before it ships. Most of the time when the checker refuses a line, my expectation was wrong, not the engine — I wrote a farewell speech recently and needed corrections on three lines where I had the reading wrong, not the synthesizer.

Smaller but satisfying: chased a layout bug where a two-column list row was quietly splitting a sentence one character at a time down a 13px column — looked exactly like intentional vertical Japanese until I measured the row heights and found one was 30x its neighbors.
